phonemes.desc: Initial sound of Þórr, as attested in the norse tradition.
Subsequent syllables preserve the name's inherited shape.

pronunciation.note: Þórr is Tier 2 because its Unicode restoration preserves the orthographic signature appropriate to the norse tradition.

domains.title: Thunder, Storms, Oak
domains.subtitle: The domain of Þórr
domains.lead: In the norse tradition, Þórr governed thunder, storms, oak. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.title: Primary Sphere
cards.body: Þórr is principally associated with thunder, storms, oak.

cards.title: Cultural Role
cards.body: Worshippers approached Þórr through cult, myth, and the material culture of the norse world.

symbols.name: Cult site
symbols.meaning: Sanctuary or holy place where Þórr was honoured

symbols.name: Ritual object
symbols.meaning: Material focus of devotion for Þórr

mythology.lead: The myths of Þórr preserve the name's power and personality across generations of retelling.

myths.title: The story of Þórr
myths.text: Þórr appears in norse tradition as a figure whose domain over thunder, storms, oak shapes both cosmic order and human experience. The surviving narratives emphasize Þórr's role, attributes, and relationships with other powers.

lore.syncretism: Norse tradition absorbed and reworked Germanic, Celtic, and Christian influences; medieval Icelandic compilers preserved the myths while Christian frameworks shaped their presentation.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name lives on in modern fantasy, Neopagan practice, Scandinavian heritage, and the global reception of Viking-Age literature. Restoring Þórr in Unicode preserves the name's cultural specificity against the flattening force of plain ASCII.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Þórr carries within it a norse understanding of thunder (from *þunraz). Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form.
sources: The Poetic Edda; The Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson.
Beekes, R. S. P. Etymological Dictionary of Greek. Leiden: Brill, 2010.
Archaeological evidence includes runestones, grave goods, place-name distributions, and Viking-Age iconography across Scandinavia and the Norse diaspora.
